# The question: recombination history

Population-genetics data usually describe chromosomes by *which* alleles they carry.
But two chromosomes with the same alleles can still differ in their **history**: one
may descend from an ancestral haplotype that has not recombined across a region, while
another is a mosaic assembled by recombination. That difference is invisible to a
single-SNP frequency, yet it is biologically meaningful — the clearest example is a
**chromosomal inversion**, where the inverted orientation suppresses recombination with
the standard one, so the two orientations accumulate distinct recombination histories.

When you have the phased genotypes of a region and suspect that this kind of hidden
structure is present, two natural questions arise:

1. *Are there groups of chromosomes with different recombination histories here?*
2. *Which part of the region is responsible for that difference?*

`recombClust` answers both. The rest of this vignette shows how, and — more importantly
— how to choose its options and read what it returns.

## How it works, in one paragraph

You do not need the details to use the package, but the intuition helps interpret the
output. `recombClust` looks at **pairs of nearby SNP-blocks**. For each pair it asks, on
every chromosome, a single question: do these two blocks look *linked* (they travel
together, as if no recombination separated them) or *independent* (recombination has
shuffled them)? The answers to many such pairs form a **recombination profile** for each
chromosome; chromosomes with a similar history end up with similar profiles, and
clustering the profiles reveals the sub-populations. The intermediate matrices are kept
in an HDF5 file rather than in memory, so the same workflow runs unchanged on large
cohorts.

```{r lib}
library(recombClust)
```

# The data you provide

`recombClust` works on a **haplotype matrix**: rows are chromosomes (phased, so each
individual contributes two rows) and columns are biallelic SNPs coded `0/1`. You would
normally build it from a VCF/GDS/BED file with `hdf5omics_import()`, which writes the
matrix to an HDF5 file and returns the SNP positions.

Here we *simulate* a region instead, for two reasons: the vignette stays self-contained,
and — because we set up the answer ourselves — you can check the output against a known
truth and learn to recognise it in your own data. We simulate 140 chromosomes over 60
SNPs with an inversion in the middle (SNPs 21-45): half of the chromosomes carry a
conserved haplotype there (recombination suppressed), the other half have recombined
freely; outside the inversion all chromosomes are equivalent.

```{r simulate}
simulate_region <- function(n = 140, nSNP = 60, inv = 21:45, mut = 0.01) {
  H <- matrix(sample(0:1, n * nSNP, replace = TRUE), n, nSNP)   # background
  label <- rep("standard", n)
  for (i in seq_len(n / 2)) {                                   # inverted chromosomes
    allele <- sample(0:1, 1)                                    # conserved haplotype
    v <- rep(allele, length(inv))
    flip <- runif(length(inv)) < mut
    v[flip] <- 1 - v[flip]
    H[i, inv] <- v
    label[i] <- "inverted"
  }
  positions <- sort(sample(seq_len(nSNP * 300), nSNP))          # bp coordinates
  list(H = H, label = label, positions = positions)
}

sim <- simulate_region()
dim(sim$H)               # chromosomes x SNPs
table(sim$label)         # the truth, hidden from the analysis

hdf5 <- tempfile(fileext = ".hdf5")
BigDataStatMeth::hdf5_create_matrix(hdf5, "haplotypes/H", data = sim$H, overwrite = TRUE)
BigDataStatMeth::hdf5_close_all()
```

`sim$label` is the answer we are pretending not to know; we will come back to it to
confirm that the analysis recovers it.

# Preparing the data: missing genotypes

Phased reference panels are usually complete, so you can often skip this step. But a
missing call cannot enter the model, and discarding SNPs or chromosomes throws away
information, so if your matrix has gaps you should fill them first with
`hdf5omics_impute()`.

The choice that matters is the **method**:

| `method`  | What it does | When to use it |
|:----------|:-------------|:---------------|
| `"ldknni"` (default) | LD-aware nearest neighbours: each missing allele is read off the most correlated SNPs and the most similar chromosomes | almost always — it respects the local haplotype structure recombClust depends on |
| `"mode"`  | the commonest allele of the SNP | a quick baseline; it ignores structure and biases allele frequencies |

`ldknni` also takes `L` (how many correlated SNPs to look at) and `k` (how many
neighbouring chromosomes to average); the defaults are sensible and rarely need
changing. Because imputation only works where there *is* linkage disequilibrium, we
demonstrate it on a matrix with realistic LD blocks, hide 5 % of the calls, and check
how many come back:

```{r impute}
ld_blocks <- do.call(cbind, lapply(rep(6, 8), function(b) {
  hap <- sample(0:1, 120, replace = TRUE)
  vapply(seq_len(b), function(j) {
    v <- hap; f <- runif(120) < 0.03; v[f] <- 1 - v[f]; v
  }, numeric(120))
}))
truth <- ld_blocks
with_missing <- ld_blocks
gaps <- sample(length(with_missing), round(0.05 * length(with_missing)))
with_missing[gaps] <- NA

fqc <- tempfile(fileext = ".hdf5")
BigDataStatMeth::hdf5_create_matrix(fqc, "hap/H", data = with_missing, overwrite = TRUE)
BigDataStatMeth::hdf5_close_all()

hdf5omics_impute(fqc, "hap", "H", out_dataset = "H_imputed", method = "ldknni")
imputed <- as.matrix(BigDataStatMeth::hdf5_matrix(fqc, "hap/H_imputed"))
BigDataStatMeth::hdf5_close_all()

mean(imputed[gaps] == truth[gaps])          # fraction recovered
```

Almost all of the hidden calls are recovered, because LD-kNNi borrows them from
correlated neighbours. In practice you would impute your haplotype file and then use the
completed matrix in the analysis below.

# Classifying chromosomes

`recombClust()` is the main entry point. You give it the haplotype file and the SNP
positions; it fits the model to every block pair, summarises the profiles with a
principal component analysis, and groups the chromosomes with k-means.

```{r pathA}
res <- recombClust(hdf5, sim$positions, clusters = 2, PCs = 3, seed = 1)
res
```

## The options and what they change

A handful of arguments let you match the analysis to your region:

| Argument     | Default | What it controls |
|:-------------|:--------|:-----------------|
| `blockSize`  | 2       | SNPs per block. Larger blocks describe longer local haplotypes but need more data per block. |
| `distance`   | 1e4     | the largest gap (bp) between the two blocks of a pair — i.e. the physical scale of linkage the model probes. Widen it to look across a larger region, narrow it to stay local. |
| `clusters`   | 2       | how many sub-populations k-means looks for. Two is the natural choice for an inversion (two orientations); raise it if you expect more groups. |
| `PCs`        | 3       | principal components kept for clustering. A few is usually enough because one dominant signal drives most of the variance. |
| `seed`       | `NULL`  | fixes the k-means start so the labelling is reproducible. |

## Reading the result

The `print` above already gives the shape of the analysis (chromosomes, number of block
pairs, cluster sizes, and the leading standard deviations — how much variance each PC
carries). The result, though, is best read as a picture:

```{r pathA-plot, fig.cap = "Each point is a chromosome, placed by its recombination profile and coloured by cluster."}
plot(res)
```

The reading is simple: **two well-separated clouds mean two distinct recombination
histories**. Here the separation is almost entirely along the first component (its
percentage in the axis label is large), which is what you expect when a single
polymorphism dominates. A single diffuse cloud, by contrast, would mean the region has
no strong recombination-history structure.

Because this is a simulation we can confirm the clusters against the truth we hid
earlier — in a real study, this labelling *is* the discovery:

```{r pathA-check}
table(truth = sim$label, cluster = res$class)
```

The clusters recover the inverted and standard chromosomes exactly. The cluster
assignment lives in `res$class` and is what you carry forward (e.g. to test association
with a phenotype).

# Locating the region

Knowing *that* the chromosomes differ, `define_Regions()` tells you *where*. It works in
two steps: `recomb_probabilities()` slides windows along the region and summarises the
recombination signal in each (kept on disk as `ModelsProb`), and `define_Regions()`
groups the windows that behave alike into blocks.

```{r pathB}
probs <- recomb_probabilities(hdf5, sim$positions, window = 800)
regions <- define_Regions(probs, CLQcut = 0.5)
regions
```

The options here control the resolution and the stringency:

| Argument    | Default | What it controls |
|:------------|:--------|:-----------------|
| `window`    | 1000    | window width (bp) in `recomb_probabilities()`. Smaller windows locate the region more finely but are noisier. |
| `CLQcut`    | 0.5     | how strong the correlation between two windows must be for them to join the same block. Raise it to report only the dominant signal, lower it to be more inclusive. |
| `clstgap`   | 40000   | a physical gap (bp) larger than this splits a block, so distant windows are not merged. |
| `minLength` | 1       | drops blocks made of fewer than this many windows. |

## Reading the result

Two complementary views help you interpret the blocks. The first is the window-by-window
correlation of the recombination signal, with the detected blocks outlined:

```{r pathB-plot, fig.cap = "Windows sharing a recombination history light up as blocks; each outline is a reported region."}
plot(regions)
```

The large block on the diagonal is the inversion: those windows share a history and are
reported as one region, whose `start`/`end` columns give its coordinates. Faint colour
off the blocks is background; smaller blocks are weaker local correlations that `CLQcut`
lets you keep or discard.

The second view places the signal on the genomic axis. Passing the cluster labels from
`recombClust()`, `plotRecombTracks()` draws the recombination proportion of each cluster
along the region and, below it, their difference; the detected regions appear as a strip:

```{r tracks, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "Recombination proportion per cluster, their difference, and the detected region along the genomic axis."}
plotRecombTracks(probs, class = res$class, regions = regions)
```

Where the two cluster lines pull apart and the difference departs from zero is exactly
the inversion — the same conclusion as the heat map, now anchored to base-pair position.
With real coordinates the per-window values feed directly into a
[Gviz](https://bioconductor.org/packages/Gviz/) `DataTrack`, so you can stack the
recombination signal against ideograms and gene models.

# A complete run from a VCF file

The walkthrough above used a simulated matrix so we could check the answer against a
known truth. In practice you start from a genotype file. The package ships a small
example VCF (a ~85 kb region of chromosome 7 for 30 individuals); `hdf5omics_import()`
turns it into an HDF5 haplotype matrix in a single call — reading, phasing and,
optionally, filtering by minor allele frequency — where earlier versions required a
chain of `VariantAnnotation`/`SnpMatrix` preprocessing:

```{r vcf}
vcf <- system.file("extdata", "example.vcf", package = "recombClust")
h <- hdf5omics_import(vcf, out_file = tempfile(fileext = ".h5"), minmaf = 0.1)
c(chromosomes = h$nchrom, SNPs = h$nsnp)
```

The returned `h` carries the HDF5 file, the dataset and the SNP positions — exactly the
inputs `recombClust()` expects:

```{r vcf-run}
fit <- recombClust(h$file, h$positions, clusters = 2, distance = 3000, seed = 1)
table(fit$class)
```

This is a small test region with no known inversion, so treat it as a demonstration of
the workflow rather than a biological finding. On a region that does carry structure,
`plot(fit)` and `define_Regions()` are read exactly as in the sections above.

# Coming from an earlier version

If you used recombClust before the 2.0 rewrite, the analysis is the same; a few entry
points were renamed or merged into cleaner ones. The table points to the current
function for each task:

| Task | Earlier versions | Now |
|:-----|:-----------------|:----|
| Load phased genotypes | `getData()` | `hdf5omics_import()` |
| Classify chromosomes | `runRecombClust()` | `recombClust()` |
| Windowed recombination probabilities | `getRecombProb()`, `computeRecombProbabilities()` | `recomb_probabilities()` |
| Detect regions | `define_Regions()` | `define_Regions()` (unchanged) |

The core model functions keep their names — `recombFreq()`, `linkageFreq()`,
`updateModel()`, `LDmixtureModel()`, `getProbs()`. The hand-written HDF5 helpers of the
older versions (creating files/groups/datasets, querying dimensions, …) are no longer
part of the package: that layer is now provided by
[BigDataStatMeth](https://github.com/isglobal-brge/BigDataStatMeth), which is what lets
the analysis run out-of-core.

# Reference

The mixture model underlying `recombClust`, and its application to real chromosomal
inversions and recombination hotspots, are described in:
